text: Lesson 5's query is syntactically correct and conceptually sound -- but Mara hasn't actually watched it fire yet. Before pointing it at Hartwell's real sign-in data, she builds three small, synthetic scenarios in Sentinel's Logs blade, each testing a different edge of the query's logic.

Scenario one: the real attack pattern. Six failed sign-ins in just over five minutes, then a success. This should produce exactly one result row -- the exact shape of someone finally guessing a phished password right.

Scenario two: the same six failures, but no success ever follows -- maybe the user gave up and called the help desk. The join against successful sign-ins finds nothing to pair with, so this correctly returns zero rows. That's correct behavior, not a bug -- this specific rule wasn't built to catch a failure cluster alone.

Scenario three: one failure, then a success two minutes later -- an everyday typo. A single failure never clears the threshold of more than five, so this also correctly returns zero rows. Without this check, every ordinary mistyped password would generate an incident, and the SOC would learn to ignore the rule within a week.

Three scenarios, three confirmations: the rule fires on the real pattern, and stays silent on both plausible near-misses. That's a stronger claim than the query ran without an error -- a query can run clean and still be wrong.
With the rule tested and trusted, next lesson writes it all down -- turning this project into a runbook the rest of the team can actually reuse.
